title: The 8 Levels of Moving Out
house: Fruit City, a bustling metropolis where produce people navigate adulting, rising rent prices, and reality checks under the glowing digital numbers on their foreheads.

A glowing golden coin is hidden near the register in the local diner.

levels.name: Pip, 19, Art Student
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 1. Level 1: 150 dollars in my pocket, and my mom just locked the front door behind me. I am Pip, a stressed green pear student wearing an oversized denim jacket and carrying a cardboard box with my entire life inside. My bank account is practically empty, and rent in this city is highway robbery. I stepped into the tiny downtown studio, my forehead glowing with my remaining cash, ready to start my independent life. You cannot afford the deposit, so get out before I call security. That stung, but I refused to cry on the dusty pavement. I reached into my coat and pulled out my grandmother's vintage gold pocket watch, hoping it would cover the first week. We don't accept family heirlooms for rent around here. She slammed the door right in my face and muttered something about broke kids. Who is going to pay for my groceries now? You'll see that in Level 2.

levels.name: Sunny, 21, Barista
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 2. Level 2: 1,100 dollars a month, and my first grocery haul cost half my paycheck. I am Sunny, an orange-peel barista in a stained apron, staring at an empty fridge in my shared flat. Moving out sounded like freedom until I realized electricity isn't free. You used the heater all night, so pay up right now or your clothes go in the dumpster. I clenched my fists, realizing I couldn't even afford pasta for the rest of the week. I tried to explain my shift schedule, but she just laughed and pointed at my forehead display. Your number is a joke, just like your excuses. That was when I noticed a strange golden coin rolling out from under her locked bedroom door. Who is actually living in that forbidden room? You'll see that in Level 3.

levels.name: Avoca, 23, Junior Copywriter
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 3. Level 3: 2,400 dollars net income, and I am still eating instant noodles every single night. I am Avoca, an avocado person working long hours at a desk job while staring at my banking app in terror. Independence felt great until my laptop broke and the repair cost wiped out my savings account. Stop rolling that chair around or I will make sure the landlord doubles your rent. I wanted to scream because I had been working overtime for three days straight just to afford my internet bill. I checked my balance again, hoping for a miracle, but it showed zero. Some of us actually want to sleep in this building. Then my phone buzzed with an alert from the bank. Why did they freeze my card right now? You'll see that in Level 4.

levels.name: Coco, 25, Graphic Designer
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 4. Level 4: 3,800 dollars a month, and I finally thought I had total control over my life. I am Coco, a brown coconut person with a hard exterior shell, living alone in a freshly painted loft. I bought my own couch, set up my Wi-Fi, and felt like a true adult. This building is losing its class with cheap rental units like yours. My blood boiled because I worked sixty hours a week for this apartment. I wanted to throw something at his immaculate shoes, but I kept my cool. Try upgrading your aesthetic before inviting guests over. He dropped a heavy delivery box on the lobby counter and walked away without a word. What was inside that mysterious package that made everyone stare? You'll see that in Level 5.

levels.name: Zelda, 28, Accountant
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 5. Level 5: 5,200 dollars salary, and I finally bought the penthouse corner apartment with the city view. I am Zelda, a sharp yellow lemon woman in a crisp blazer, enjoying my morning espresso on the balcony. I mastered budgets, taxes, and independent living. Turn that down or I'm calling the building manager right now! I rolled my eyes because my playlist was barely audible over the traffic. People with low numbers always find something to complain about instead of working harder. Some of us have to work early shifts while you party! I slammed my glass balcony door shut and ignored her childish tantrum. Who dared to threaten my peaceful lifestyle? You'll see that in Level 6.

levels.name: Kiwi, 32, Project Manager
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 6. Level 6: 7,400 dollars monthly income, and I just bought a two-story townhouse in the best neighborhood. I am Kiwi, a fuzzy brown kiwi person in a tailored green suit, unpacking crystal glasses in my new kitchen. Moving out years ago was tough, but now I own my space. You only bought this place because your family helped with the down payment, right? That remark infuriated me because every single dollar came from my own brutal overtime work. I wanted to throw him out right then and there. Don't pretend you did it all on your own. He dropped a crumpled office memo on my kitchen island and stormed out. What secret information was hidden inside that memo? You'll see that in Level 7.

levels.name: Drax, 36, Real Estate Mogul
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 7. Level 7: 12,500 dollars passive income every month, and I own half the residential blocks in this city. I am Drax, a pink and green dragonfruit man in an expensive bespoke suit, signing property deeds in my executive office. I conquered the real estate market long ago and despise amateur mistakes. Your latest building project looks outdated and lacks any real architectural vision! That insolence made my blood boil because I built this empire from scratch. I slammed my gold-plated pen onto the mahogany desk and stared him down. Even empires crumble when the foundation is rotten. He slid a confidential financial audit across the table and smirked. What shocking truth was revealed in those documents? You'll see that in Level 8.

levels.name: Madam Peach, 45, Real Estate Queen
levels.story: The 8 levels of moving out. Level 8. Level 8: 15,000 dollars daily revenue, and I own every single building where all of you started your journey. I am Madam Peach, a sleek peach woman in a velvet suit, standing in the grand penthouse overlooking Fruit City. I watched every single one of you struggle, fight, and claw your way out of Hotel Mama just to reach the top. We finally made it to the top floor, Madam Peach. The young pear student I threw out on day one? He just bought the commercial block right across the street. The number on your forehead never defines your hustle, but it always tells the truth about where you are headed. The number never lies. I poured a glass of vintage wine and smiled as the entire city skyline lit up with digital numbers below. Which topic of our fruit and vegetable universe should we explore in the next epic series?
